# Wheel of the Year

A Skill Harbor house build for people who live by the seasons, and for the curious who want to discover the wheel one festival at a time. Wheel of the Year does not predict anything, and it says so in its first line. The solstices and equinoxes it works with are astronomy: exact dates and times for 2026 and 2027, cross-checked between two published sources, with the source and the timezone stated. The eight festivals around them, Imbolc, Ostara, Beltane, Litha, Lughnasadh, Mabon, Samhain and Yule, and everything the tradition associates with them, are presented as tradition, from pagan, Wiccan and folkloric sources, never as facts or promises.

It starts by asking what your wheel looks like. All eight festivals, or only a few? Northern hemisphere, or southern, where the wheel shifts by six months? Which practices are yours: a simple ritual, a seasonal meal, time in nature, writing only? Then your Muse watches the calendar for you: an alert seven days before each chosen festival so you can prepare, and another the day before, with the exact time when the festival is a solstice or an equinox.

Around each festival you dictate short journal entries; after it, the assistant reads them back and asks for your verdict: resonated, did not resonate, or in between. After a full wheel it counts from your own journal alone, festival by festival, and asks what you want to keep, drop or change. Everything stays in a folder on your device.
